headline: High Court refused MACC's bid to freeze RM548m linked to Na'imah in Singapore
context: On 22 May 2026, the KL High Court refused MACC's application for a Section 53 order to freeze £21 million and US$99 million (about RM548m) held in Singapore and alleged to be linked to Na'imah Abdul Khalid, widow of the late Tun Daim Zainuddin, and eight others. MACC says it will appeal.

cards.big: MACC's hunt for assets linked to Daim Zainuddin's family looked sweeping: RM3 billion traced across 11 countries, Ilham Tower seized, accounts chased from London to Singapore.
cards.sub: Then on 22 May 2026 a judge refused to freeze about RM548m of it in Singapore, and spelled out where the case fell short.

cards.big: High Court judge Mohd Arief Emran Arifin dismissed the bid, ruling the prosecution had not met the threshold Section 53 of the anti-money-laundering act sets.
cards.sub: Section 53 lets a court bar dealing with assets held abroad while a case runs. The judge found the evidence for that bar too thin.

cards.big: Malaysia's drive to lock down the overseas money keeps meeting court limits: London granted a £132m freeze in June 2025, then stayed it; Singapore refused outright.
cards.sub: Each check leaves the assets under no Malaysian freeze while MACC litigates. It has 14 days to appeal.

cards.big: Announced scope and proven guilt are different things. Daim was discharged and acquitted after his death; the wider case remains unproven.
cards.sub: His widow Na'imah is contesting a 2024 asset-declaration charge, now before the Federal Court. The dismissal judged the freeze, not whether the money is clean.

cards.big: A seizure announced is not money recovered. Between the press conference and the recovered ringgit sits a proof threshold the state has yet to clear.
Think of it as tracing money you suspect is tainted, then being told you have not shown enough to stop the account holders touching it while the case runs.
Asset recovery turns on proving provenance to the law's threshold, not the size of the number announced. The appeal decides whether the money can be frozen, not who keeps it.
